readerTitle: A $30,000 logo and the same 1 in 5
caseNote: 가상 사례 (IT 지원 회사, 사내 데이터 분석팀) · 모든 수치는 설명용 + 브랜드를 기억 구조로 보는 마케팅 연구 관점 (Sharp)
insight: 브랜드는 로고나 디자인 파일이 아니라 사람들 머릿속에 쌓인 기대이고, 그 기대는 매번의 경험이 만든다.
misconception: 브랜드는 이름, 로고, 웹사이트이며 디자인을 새로 하면 브랜드가 바뀐다.

sources.text: Sharp, B. (2010). How Brands Grow. Oxford University Press. (브랜드를 구매자 머릿속의 기억 구조로 보는 관점)
Northline 및 사내 분석팀 사례와 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 수주율 1 in 5 = 20%, 1 in 3 ≈ 33%(차트에는 33으로 표기). 로고 교체 전후 모두 20%로 변화 없음을 보여주는 것이 목적입니다.
'브랜드 = 머릿속 기억과 기대'라는 정의는 Sharp(2010) 등 마케팅 연구의 일반적 관점으로 서술했습니다. 특정 인용문은 쓰지 않았습니다. 게시 전 4번 카드의 표현이 원 관점과 어긋나지 않는지 확인하세요.
Bezos, Ogilvy 등에게 흔히 귀속되는 브랜드 정의 인용문은 출처가 불확실해 의도적으로 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: A $30,000 logo and the same 1 in 5
body: Northline, a small IT support firm, paid $30,000 for a new logo, new colors and a new website.
Six months later it still won about 1 in 5 of the proposals it sent. A rival with a plain, dated logo won about 1 in 3, and charged more.

image.label: A shiny new logo on a sign above an empty office
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 반짝이는 새 간판이 걸린 작은 사무실, 안은 조용함. 옆 건물에는 낡고 소박한 간판인데 사람들이 줄 서 있음. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: You run Northline. What do you do next?
body: The new look didn't move the win rate. Your rival wins more deals at a higher price. You have budget for one move this quarter.

options.text: Hire a better agency and refresh the look again
options.feedback: You'd get a sharper look, but if the look wasn't the problem, you'd spend another $30,000 on the wrong thing.

options.text: Ask lost prospects and current clients how they'd describe you, then fix what they say
options.feedback: It's slower and less exciting than a redesign, but it tells you what people actually expect from you, which is where choices are made.

options.text: Cut prices 10% to win more proposals
options.feedback: You may win some deals, but you'd teach the market that you're the cheap option, and that memory is hard to undo.

cards.title: What the new logo didn't move
body: Northline called ten prospects who chose the rival. Nobody mentioned logos. They said things like "they pick up the phone" and "they fixed my friend's server on a Sunday."

image.label: What the new logo didn't move
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: A brand is what people expect from you.
body: **A brand** is the set of memories and expectations people hold about a business. It lives in customers' heads, not in the design files.
Marketing researchers describe it this way: when a buyer thinks of a need, certain names come to mind, along with what each one is like. Those memories shape the choice.
The logo is a label. The memory behind it is the brand.

image.label: A logo as a small tag on a big bundle of memories
image.brief: 머리 실루엣 안에 기억 말풍선들("Answers fast", "Fixed it on Sunday", "My friend uses them"). 그 묶음에 작은 이름표처럼 로고 태그가 달려 있음. 실제 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Every contact leaves a memory.
body: The rival never ran a brand campaign. Its brand was built from small moments like these:
list: How fast someone answers the phone
What one client tells another over lunch
cards.callout: Each moment adds to the memory or takes away from it. A redesign changes none of them.

cards.title: You have a brand whether you manage it or not.
body: A freelancer has one. So does a corner shop, a supplier and a team inside a company. If people hold expectations about you, that's your brand.
The only question is whether you know what those expectations are and whether they're the ones you want.
cards.softwareNote: In software, the brand is mostly the product itself: how fast it loads, how bugs get handled, how support replies. Users often form their memory in the first session, long before they see your marketing.

cards.title: Names and logos still matter, just differently.
body: A logo can't create a good memory. But it helps people find and recognize one. A great firm that nobody can tell apart from others leaks value too. (More on this in *distinctive assets*.)
Also, memories change slowly. Fixing response times today may take months to show up in what people say about you. Judge the effort by what clients say, not by next week's numbers.

cards.title: Now it's a team inside a company.
body: You lead the data analytics team at a large retailer. Other departments call your team "the black hole": requests go in, nothing comes out. Many now build their own messy spreadsheets instead of asking you.

options.text: Rename the team "Insights Hub" and launch a new intranet page
options.feedback: It feels like a fresh start, but a new label on the same slow experience can make the old memory feel even more true.

options.text: Promise a reply to every request within two days, keep it, and share what you delivered
options.feedback: It costs time and focus, but it replaces the memory people actually hold, one request at a time.

options.text: Ask leadership to require that all data requests go through you
options.feedback: You'd get the work back, but not the goodwill. People who are forced to use you still expect the black hole.

cards.title: Your brand is the memory people carry, not the logo you chose.
body: Change the experience and the memory follows. Change only the look and the memory stays.
**Try it today:** ask three customers or colleagues to describe your business in five words. Compare their words with the ones you'd want.
